utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam Registrar. Good afternoon, everybody else. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. All the accused are here. Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Ostojic and Mr. Bourgon. Prosecution is -- I see Mr. McCloskey, I see Mr. Nicholls and Mr. Vanderpuye. The witness is already in the courtroom. So I take it we can proceed. General, we are going to proceed with your cross-examinations today, and I'm confident that we will finish with your testimony relatively soon. Yes. Please remember that the solemn declaration still holds good, and that in addition you ought to keep in mind what I told you when you first started giving evidence, about your right to ask not to answer some questions that may be put to you. So good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General. I would kindly ask Exhibit number P192 to be brought up on the screen for the witness. Can we scroll up the document to show bullet point number 4? Thank you. General, we have talked a lot about this document. On the assumption that you drafted it and sent it to the addresses indicated in the document, would the conclusion on the role of General Miletic with regard to bullet point number 4 be that he was only conveying the information that he received from the assistant commander for security and intelligence? Could you please look at the document?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. This means that he was supposed to inform the commander of the Main Staff of the existence of the document, of its contents, and to seek from the commander his explanation as to whether he accepted those proposals or not and to provide him with some information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In other words, just to convey the information?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now kindly ask the usher, before I proceed with my next questions, to provide the witness with three documents that I will be presenting to him in a row, because it seems to me that it would be much easier for everybody if we proceeded that way than if we decided to put these documents next to each other on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, you know that the documents pertaining to command orders, directives, as a special type of order and instructions, you're familiar with all those?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Based on the general knowledge that you have on the command documents, could you conclude that the common denominators for all these documents is that the subordinated officers have to carry out the orders, commands and directives received from the superior command without any alterations to them or challenging them?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please see Exhibit P0005 on e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, you see the document on the screen, and in the heading of the document you can see that it was issued by the Supreme Command of the armed forces of Republika Srpska on 8 March 1995.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please look at the last page of this document? We have a problem here. Can we have page 3179 in the B/C/S version? Can we scroll up a little to see the signature on the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, you will agree with me, won't you, that this document was issued by the Supreme Commander, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, and that this document is signed?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, signed and stamped.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Under bullet point 8 on the same page, you can see that this document was drafted by Colonel Radivoje Miletic?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: On the last page, page number 3181, you can see that the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, on the 17th of March 1995, as very urgent, sent the directive number 7, which is the document that we have been discussing, through the Chief of Staff, Lieutenant General Manojlo Milovanovic, sent it to the command of the Krajina Corps, of the 1st Krajina Corps, that is?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I suppose that this document was also sent to all the other operative units, but here we can see that this was sent to the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. We have confirmation from the 1st Krajina Corps here. Also you will agree with me that the directive, as a form of document, is sent only to the operative organs, in this case corps, of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to the operative units or operative systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now move to page 3173 of this directive number 7? I apologise, 3171 is the page number.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: One of the components of every directive is the thing that you see under bullet point number 5, which is the tasks of the units?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: If we now move two pages further, and if we come to page number 3173, if you could please look at that page, you will see that the Supreme Command, in other words, the supreme commander of that command at the time, President Dr. Radovan Karadzic, issued a task to the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: That task issued to the Drina Corps was as follows: "To carry out a physical separation of Srebrenica and Zepa in order to prevent communication between these two enclaves, and this should be carried out as soon as possible."

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is exactly what the tasks -- the task says.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In other words, the Drina Corps was a unit subordinated to the Main Staff, and also it was subordinated to the Supreme Command, i.e. to the Supreme Commander?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through the Main Staff. It was not directly subordinated to the Supreme Command or the Supreme Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When it comes to the Drina Corps, was it duty-bound to fully and without any alterations, modifications, convey the task that they had received from the Supreme Command to their subordinated units?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their duty was to convey the task in the form it was received, without any alterations to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now bring up on e-court Exhibit number P838?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, you have that document under tab -- have you found it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can we then agree that this document was issued by the command of the Drina Corps on 2nd July 1995, and that it was sent to the commands of the 1st Zvornik Brigade, the 1st Bircani Brigade, the 2nd Romanija Brigade, the 1st Bratunac Brigade, the 1st Milici Brigade and to the 5th Mixed Artillery Regiment? The title of the document is, "Order for active combat activity, OP number 1." Also, we will agree, won't we, that in the right-hand corner, it is indicated, "Military secret, strictly confidential," copy number illegible, probably 3?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so, most probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And that there is the code name Krivaja 95. Is all that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, everything is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can we now move to the last page of this document? Can we scroll up a little in order to show the signature? On the last page of the document, in the right corner, it says, "Commander, Major General Milenko Zivanovic"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can we now go to page 2 of the document? Please look at the bullet point 2 of the document, where on page 2 in the B/C/S version, and in the English version it is on page 3 also, paragraph 2, it says that the command of the Drina Corps issues this order quoting directives number 7 and 7/1. Further on, under this bullet point, can we agree that it says that the Drina Corps is tasked with separating the enclaves Srebrenica and Zepa as soon as possible and narrow both of them down to their inner urban areas?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is exactly what one can read under item 2 of this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at directive number 7 and let's go back to page 3173 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I apologise, just one clarification on what I think is an important translation mistake. It should be narrow down the enclaves to its urban areas. Been translated for years as urban areas, not inner areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you agree to that, Madam Fauveau or Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the original directive, i.e. the order, it is indicated "urban area" in the order that I have shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then we can proceed. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. McCloskey and thank you, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Could we see document P5, please? Exhibit P5?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, sir, now you have this directive before you directive 7 and the order of General Zivanovic dated the 2nd of July. If you look at directive 7, you will see that it issues a task to carry out complete physical separation of Srebrenica and Zepa, prevent individual communication between these two enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And if you now take a look at the order of General Zivanovic dated the 2nd of July, we see that in paragraph 2, as a task given to the unit, I'm now referring to item 2 of this order, what is stated there, is that the order specifying the task to the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 2 of the order, as a combat document, command document, from the level of a squad until the strategic level, is always the task given by the superior command and it cannot be changed. So this is something that is received from the superior command. This is the task and it is literally copied down. It cannot be altered in any way. The task has been defined by the document issued by the superior command, and that's final.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So the directive given in directive 7 to carry out complete physical separation of Srebrenica and Zepa and prevent individual communication between these two enclaves is the task that the commander of the Drina Corps has to include under item 2?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So based on what we have here, based on these two documents, one could conclude that the commander of the Drina Corps gave up or rather he altered the task in relation to the task he had received from the superior command?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. He altered the substance of the task. The task was clearly defined, the task given to him, namely to carry out complete physical separation of Srebrenica and Zepa by way of which they would also prevent the individual communication between these two enclaves. That was his task, not narrowing them down to any territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see P361 in e-court, please? I apologise, 5D361. Yes. That's the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, sir, this is the document issued by the General Staff of the army of Republika Srpska on the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska on the 31st of March 1995. It is entitled, "Directive for further action, OPBR 7/1"?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could we now see the last page of this directive, please? Would you agree that this directive was issued by Lieutenant-General Mladic and that it was prepared by Colonel Radivoje Miletic?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could we see page 8781?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would object to this line of inquiry to the extent that I think it grossly exceeds the extent of the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But our rules do not limit cross-examination only to questions or issues raised during the examination-in-chief. It's within our discretion to stop or let Mr. Petrusic go ahead with the questions. I can understand your concern in a way but because I think the questions could be shortened and the issues dealt with in a much more direct manner, but we are not going to stop Mr. Petrusic. Go ahead, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, sir, you can see here that item 5 lists the tasks given to the units and on the next page, 8782, we can see the task given to the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Now, would you please read the task under 5/3?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Item 5/3, the Drina Corps. By way of persistent defence and active combat operation at the northwest part of the front and around enclaves, prevent further incursion of the enemy in selected -- selective -- selected operative and tactical directions and by way of evident action and by applying measures of operative and tactical camouflaging, involve as many forces of the enemy as possible. In concert with IBK, as soon as possible, implement the tasks given in the operation Spreca 95 and in the first phase of the operation, reach the line going from Vis to Kalesija and further on carry out regrouping of forces and in concert with the forces of IBK, 1st KK and air force and air defence in the second and third phase of the operation by using an appropriate manoeuvre and by putting into action strong groups in the rear of the enemy lines, and by introducing stronger armoured and mechanised forces, carry out an attack on the general axis, Kalesija-Dubrava-Tuzla and as soon as possible reach the line between the village of Serici, Zivinice, Jasicak, Ravno Brdo, and in this way cut off the forces of the 2nd Corps of the so-called army of Bosnia-Herzegovina south of the said line.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have the English translation. This was on-sight translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you will agree that this task does not mention by a single word Krivaja 95 or anything else relating to any combat activities in relation to Srebrenica or Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except for these words, "By persistent defence." There is nothing else to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could it be concluded that the commander of the Drina Corps did not have any basis when, in his order, in item 7 [as translated], he invoked directive 7/1?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I object to this question on two grounds. First it calls for speculation and secondly it calls for an expert opinion of this witness he cannot testify to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I stand to be corrected by my colleagues, but I don't think we are with you. I think the question as it is is asking the witness whether the invocation of or the reference to directive 7/1 in the order to the commander of the Drina Corps was misplaced. I don't think it's calling for speculation. So, General, please if you could answer that question, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is so obvious that the commander of the Drina Corps altered the task that no expertise is needed to establish this. This is simply evident on the face of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correction for the transcript, page 10, line 25, there should be instead of "number 7" it should be item 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Let's proceed to your next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, we will not be dealing with this topic any longer. While you were on sick leave, your Chief of Staff, Lieutenant-Colonel Jazic stood in for you?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was also deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did he carry out his basic duty of Chief of Staff during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He carried out both the duty of the Chief of Staff and served as the commander of the regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Is that a general rule?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the general rule. If a commander or some other senior officer is unable to discharge his duties, then another person will replace him as provided by the establishment rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: While you were absent and while you were replaced by your Chief of Staff, in cases when he was absent as well, who would substitute for him?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, this can be regulated in two ways. One way is for the commander to designate a senior officer who would replace him while he's absent if we are dealing with a shorter period of time. And then there is an unwritten rule, especially during war, that when the commander is absent, and when his deputy is absent, the assistant commander for logistics serves as the most senior officer. This is done for a very practical reason. When the command post is developed within the combat order, it has at least two elements. It serves as the basic command post where the command group is located, headed by the commander, chief of staff and the entire staff. And then in the logistics command post, which is separated -- separated, it's detached, they are not next to each other, there is the assistant commander for logistics together with his logistics organ and chiefs of various services. The security organ and the organ for moral guidance, religious and legal affairs, can be located either -- in either of those two command posts. Since combat operations inevitably incur losses should the command post be destroyed, should the command group be neutralised, this is the mechanism that was developed, namely for the assistant commander for logistics to take over as the most senior officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In July of 1995, General Manojlo Milovanovic served as the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Milovanovic was the Chief of Staff from May 1992 until sometime in 1996, including July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: What we know is that during that period of time, that is to say July 1995, was absent from the command post in Crna Rijeka, and he was located at the forward command post of the 2nd Krajina Corps, where he led certain operations. That is to say, in the western part of the front. Did his -- was his post of Chief of Staff terminated when he was moved from the main command post to the command post number 2?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Logically speaking, his post was not terminated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Very well, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do not have any further questions for this witness. My cross-examination is completed. General, sir, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Petrusic. Mr. Josse? Do you still require 40 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At least 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: General, I'm asking questions on behalf of General Gvero. You have been asked various questions about your military career and indeed Mr. Petrusic dealt with the period up to July 2002 when you retired from the VRS. I'm not sure anyone has asked you what rank you were when you retired.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was retired as a Lieutenant General.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And it's right, isn't it, that you had a very distinguished war record, which included being the youngest Lieutenant-Colonel in the VRS, being appointed at the age of 35; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not really go into any statistics, but I believe so. I believe you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And as you've alluded in the course of your evidence, you were wounded on a number of occasions, but on each of those occasions you returned to the battlefield after a period of convalescence?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And it's the 1995 battle in Zepa that I want to ask you a bit more about. You've already told the Chamber a certain amount about your activities there between the 15th and the 25th of July of that year, and in particular, your activities at Brezova Ravan. How many men were under your personal command when you were at that position?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under my personal command, I had parts of the motorised battalion who were permanently holding that position. There were some 200 plus men. And 30 members of the military police, whom, after the attack against the command post, I sent to the reconnaissance missions that I spoke about yesterday. In other words, let me sum it up, I had up to 250 men under my direct command.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And some of these men, am I right in saying, you had collected or had been sent to you from the Sarajevo region?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't collect them. I issued an order to the effect that from the strength of the combat group that was in the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo Corps that the most experienced and the best fighters, a total of 30 of them, should report at the command post in Crna Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And these are what in English we would call crack troops. I hope that translates properly.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You might call them that. According to our rules, the rules that we applied, when it comes to carrying out certain tasks in order to take fortified objects or facilities, you do form something that you might call crack groups, as you call them in English, in order to perform those tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You had already seen action in Zepa in 1992, as you told the Chamber yesterday, and you were aware of how difficult the terrain in that area is to fight, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The terrain was really difficult. Let me just illustrate by saying that the village of Zepa is at an altitude of some 300 metres above the sea level, and that straight above Zepa is Zlovrh facility which is about 1500 metres above the sea level, which means that the difference between the two is about 1200 metres. All the other facilities are at a somewhat lower level. Still very perpendicular to the ground, which does not allow the use of tanks or other artillery equipment. According to some standards that were applied in the JNA, we usually had mountain units that were sent to carry out tasks in such difficult conditions and on the ground that did not really lend itself to an easy advancement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Since you couldn't use tanks or heavy artillery equipment, perhaps you could briefly describe the sort of weaponry that was at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to the small arms that every foot soldier normally has, and certain quantity of equipment for close battle that you can also use against the fortified facility such as bunkers, yesterday I already said that I had sent a request to the Drina Corps and from their units I formed two fire units for direct fire support. I had two 120-millimetre mortars and two cannons. Such tools could be carried by the soldiers. They could be disassembled and then reassembled in place in order to launch an attack and to open fire on different features.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The two cannons that you've just mentioned, were these B-1 cannons that you had got from the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The B-1 cannons were from the strength of the Rogatica Brigade and as for the 120-millimetre mortars, those were from the equipment of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What happened to these cannons?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made an assessment of the situation and I was thinking of how to neutralise the fire from the enemy, and I concluded that this would be best done by opening fire from the Boksanica sector which is also very difficult ground, forested ground, and that's why I sent a request to the commander of the Rogatica brigade, i.e. to the command of the Drina Corps, to mobilise on the 14th of July and in the night between 14 and 15 July, the [indiscernible] to disassemble the equipment and to carry it to the place. This was done with some difficulties so on the 15th, we opened cannon fire and we eliminated the combat security of the enemy in the Gusanica sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That conveniently, General, leads me to ask you about your assessment of the weaponry that Colonel Palic had at his disposal in trying to repel your attack. What weapons did you see the ABiH have?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once when we opened fire, we concluded, and also based on some previous intelligence, we concluded that they had small arms, infantry weapons, that they also had anti-armour weapons such as hand-held mortars, 60, 72 millimetres, that they had machine-guns and that they had light rocket launchers, 128 millimetres. This is what we concluded based on the fire that they opened. This was not our guess work. We could see that. We could observe that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you see or infer from the artillery that your men was receiving whether Colonel Palic's men had any UNPROFOR weapons at their disposal?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They had taken over their check-points and their entire equipment or weaponry and they used all that in fighting our forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Can you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The arms that UNPROFOR had, they took over. The check-points of the UNPROFOR were well-fortified features that was fortified with sandbags, which usually repels infantry fire very well, as well as hand-held grenades. So there is very difficult to come up with something that could neutralise those fortifications. Whatever they could hold up they used it. Since this was a Ukrainian battalion, they had BTR transporters. They had 7.62 millimetres infantry weapons, and these were the weapons that were used that had been taken from the UNPROFOR. They also had machine-guns that they had taken from them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Could we have, Mr. Josse, a date, if it's within the witness's knowledge, when this arsenal sort of was appropriated or misappropriated by Palic's men from the Ukrainian Bat or UNPROFOR? And having established that, then I need to address another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You've heard the question of the learned Judge, and you've also already told us, General, that you only arrived in Zepa on the 15th of July. Bearing in mind those two matters, can you assist as to when this weaponry had been seized from the Ukrainian Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, let me answer your question. According to the intelligence information that we had, the weaponry was seized before any combat operations that were displayed by the Republika Srpska army against the Zepa Brigade, and I could see that the -- that this was true as of the 15th of July when we were engaged in immediate combat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The other thing is I just want to make sure that between 1992, when he was first engaged in the Zepa area, and mid-July 1995, when he was engaged again there, he was never engaged there in any combat activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I in fact think the witness was engaged there in the intervening period. Let me ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In fact, you fought there between 1992 and 1995, you saw action there in 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I spoke about that yesterday partly. After a series of attacks, provocations, infliction of losses upon the army and the civilian population in 1992, finally in August 1992, for the first time, we responded to the fire opened by the Muslim forces in Zepa, and these activities went on up to the autumn of that year. Since this is mountain terrain and winter comes very early, there is a lot of snowfall, the Main Staff issued a decision that the forces of the Motorised Battalion should come closer to the populated areas and villages populated by the Serbian population. The reason for that was the long winter and a lot of snowfall and this would have enabled them to provide logistical support to the units on the front line. Your Honours, I always had a unit that was facing the Zepa sector because of the vicinity of Zepa and the command post of the Main Staff. In other words, we were continuously in contact of sorts up to the year 1995. I was not always personally there. I was not always present. But that unit of mine that I've just referred to, that unit was always there in close contact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My next question, over these years, the interim period between 1992 and 1995, were you in a position to notice any particular difference in the arsenal of the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in conflicts that were renewed sometime in May 1993, for the first time from the Muslim combat positions we could notice fire being opened from some pieces that we had not been able to register up to then. We are talking about mortars, 60 and 82 millimetres and light rocket launchers, 128 millimetres. Yes, now this has been recorded. This is actually a light rocket launcher which is one barrel of a multi-barrelled rocket launcher which is intended for opening fire in this particular type of area, and on this particular type of terrain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about anti-aircraft weaponry? Are you aware of any of that being used against your forces, and if so, what was the source of that weaponry?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In one attack on the radio relay hub Veliki Zep which I believe was at the beginning of August 1992, the Muslim forces captured 13 soldiers of the army of Republika Srpska with their complete weaponry that they had at that feature, and amongst them was an anti-aircraft system Strela 2-M. I can't remember how many systems there were but they had them and I also believe that they had 20-millimetre cannons but I can't be sure of that and I can't claim that for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, dealing with the enemy, when you were there in 1995 in particular, how would you assess the capability of the Zepa Brigade to deal with the difficult terrain that you have described?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This terrain was always much more conducive for defence, and members of the Zepa Brigade were familiar with it, very familiar with it, and they applied a tactic that absolutely prevented the army of Republika Srpska to prevail in any elements they excluded the use of support systems because their defence positions were positioned in the forested ground which completely excluded any fire support on the side of the army of Republika Srpska and prevented the Republika Srpska army from opening fire with support on such features.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What was your state of knowledge when you arrived in the Zepa area in mid-July of 1995 as to where the Zepa civilian population was at that point?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have information about that. I only knew that in that part, there was a hot line between some structures on the Muslim side, and some structures on the Serb side and some parts of the UNPROFOR. They were heavily involved in smuggling of some things that were in short supply. I didn't know anything apart from that. I only knew that there was a shortage of certain goods, certain foodstuffs, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the answer you gave, it may be that my question wasn't very happily phrased, it was also translated slightly inaccurately. Let me be more specific. Did you have any knowledge of the fact that the population of the village of Zepa had left the village and had actually gone up in the mountains in order to take refuge?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's a different story. The terrain is such that from the village of Zepa towards the River Drina - I believe that the villages are called Slabi Pripecak - the terrain is such that you can go behind the Zlovrh feature and the population or anybody who stays there is safe from any fire activity because they are protected by that high elevation, by that high rising ground, and they cannot be threatened.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And can you confirm that there were intelligence reports within the VRS that the population had gone to those places?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, I want to return briefly, if I may, to the cannons and I want to ask you about an incident on the 24th of July when you reached Brezova Ravan and what happened to two of your cannons.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not my cannons. They were from the Bratunac Brigade. As they were moving from one firing position to another, they came to the sector of Brezova Ravan, and while they were being deployed at that new firing position, fire was opened from the top of a rock in Vratar village behind the village of Zepa. As a result of that fire, in a split second I saw a fire, and I managed to find shelter at the last moment, and the cannon crews did not notice the same fire at that moment, that 128-millimetre rocket launcher opened fire with tragic consequences for both crews. In other words, all the men were killed on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And was the cannon destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were not destroyed, because fire opened from the light rocket launcher is not that powerful. It has a lot of shrapnel, which inflict consequences upon the manpower rather than the equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At some point in time, you were with General Mladic whilst this fighting at Brezova Ravan was going on, and he commented to you about its ferocity. If that's right, please tell the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. He simply could not believe how fierce that defence was until the moment he arrived at the place where I was and then he personally convinced himself that the fire was really strong and then he realised that we could not go on like that. That's why I said that the battle for this Brezova Ravan feature lasted for some 10 days or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And presumably, General Mladic was there simply viewing the attack; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. He found himself there for a simple reason. The other units from the Drina Corps that had been given their tasks and axes of attack did not achieve any results for days. They could not move. They could not advance. Then he saw by observing the situation that this was very difficult. That's why he came to the spot, to see what the reason was and why the task could not be accomplished within the specified space of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Two other specific matters in relation to Zepa. The first is: Do you have any knowledge of attempts by the VRS to disarm UNPROFOR troops at check-point 2?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any information to that effect. I believe that in some of the reports by the army of Republika Srpska, this may be mentioned but let me put it this way: This was not an attempt to disarm UNPROFOR. At this check-point, at Boksanica, this check-point served as the first point of contact for radio communication between the commander of the Zepa Brigade and the commander of the Rogatica Brigade who knew each other from before the war. The commander of the Ukrainian Battalion was there, Dudnik, and he was the one who through whom this went. No UNPROFOR members were disarmed. They were not attacked. Their base, to call it that way, this check-point, was used in order to establish communication and to start communicating with the officers of the Zepa Brigade and later on, the local authorities of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were you injured in this campaign, that is the 1995 Zepa campaign?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was in 1992, on the 4th of September. That's when I was wounded, in that Zepa campaign.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: One other matter in relation to Zepa, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. In my mind I think this needs some clarification. Yesterday, when was testifying he explained that until a particular day in June of 1995, he was in hospital for a long period of time, I think from October until June, which would take it October 1994 to June 1995, if that is correct. And the reason for that, he said that he had suffered some -- he was injured. So now he's saying he was injured in 1992 but he must have been injured again later on. If he would repeat -- would explain --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. I dealt with that in absolute summary at the beginning of my questions. I'm more than happy to ask the witness to deal with it this in detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think he needs to because the way you have put it in his answer that now begs the other question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: General, perhaps bearing in mind the question or the observation of the learned Presiding Judge, you could go through relatively briefly the occasions you were injured during the course of the war of 1992 to 1995, how long it took you to convalesce and briefly what those injuries were?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was wounded for the first time on the 4th of September 1992, as I have told you, in clashes with the then-forces of the 4th of June from Zepa. That recovery period lasted some 20 days or so. I'm not sure. But I have my entire medical documentation, and if necessary, you can verify this. The second time I was wounded slightly, in May of 1992 and that did not require hospitalisation. In May of 1993. The third time, as I've told you, was on the 12th of October 1994, and that was the most serious injury. I left the hospital at my own request. I wasn't done with my treatment. And until the very end I had to deal with the consequences of that wounding, which are basically permanent. So those were the three instances of me being wounded, just to avoid any confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So far as these troops in the Zepa Brigade were concerned, were many of them huntsmen by trade and therefore rather good shots?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But before I answer that question, just another remark concerning your previous question. The three instances of me being wounded did not all occur in the Zepa sector, to avoid any confusion. I wasn't involved in combat only there. As for your next question, my answer was yes, and I know this for a fact. I'm not speculating. As I told you yesterday, I was born in Sokolac but my parents lived in Han Pijesak, which borders part of the Zepa enclave. As a boy, I went with my father to the Muslim villages because my father used to be a driver by profession. A number of my friends who worked in police before the war, both Serbs and Muslims, very frequently told me stories, practically hunting heroic acts of those people who had a liberal attitude towards the law when it came to hunting regulations. They would frequently engage in unlawful activity regarding that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And here is my much-promised last topic in relation to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we have a look at 6D49, please? In fact, it's going to be the report that begins at the bottom of that page, so we see it's the 30th of October 1994. Up a little please. And we see it's a report from the police security station in Zepa to the RBH Ministry of the Interior in Sarajevo. And if we could go thereafter to the second page at the bottom in the B/C/S, and it's page 3 in the middle in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And the bit I'm going to take you to is about - no, right down at the bottom, please. That's it, thank you - is the bit that we see there that refers to the 8th operation group. Have you got that? It's about ten lines up from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It goes on the way the Luka company operated, now is the important bit, and the negotiations carried out by the commander of the local brigade at Boksanica without the knowledge of the Presidency of the Zepa municipality, during which the autonomy of Zepa, those three words being in inverted commas, in the so-called Republika Srpska was discussed. I want to ask you, General, whether you new anything about this proposal for the autonomy of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday, when I answered certain questions, I said that upon arrival to the command post of the regiment on the 23rd of June 1995, I was briefed about the situation in the unit, as well as in the area surrounding the unit, focusing on areas where the regiment forces were deployed, including the Zepa sector. I was informed in general terms about the fact that there were some negotiations underway, negotiations between our forces and the Zepa representatives, about resolving the problem in that part of the territory to the satisfaction of both parties. So it's not like I had some specific knowledge about people who were involved and the places. I just knew about it in general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And beyond what you've already said and beyond what this document reports, can you give the Trial Chamber any more detail?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I didn't know all the details. I didn't know everything to the full extent. I just knew that there was such an activity and that it was underway. Now, who led it, both on our side and on the other side, I didn't know that because I wasn't involved in it, so I didn't inquire about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm moving on to a discrete topic which will take me about 15 minutes. It's totally unrelated to what I've asked about hitherto. I'd request the break now, if it meets with the Court's agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have the break now. And it will be of 25 minutes' duration, starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: General, you were asked yesterday by Mr. Vanderpuye to give your assessment of a number of the gentlemen who are in the dock in this particular case. For whatever reason, you weren't asked to give an assessment of General Gvero, and that's the area that I wish to turn to now. And perhaps we could put up on e-court 1D196. Whilst that's being done, this is the interview under caution that you gave at the Banja Luka field office of this Tribunal on the 17th of October of 2005. You were interviewed by an investigator and also by Mr. McCloskey. I'm going to go through the short passage where you talk about General Gvero, and brief preamble if I may, I'm not seeking to embarrass either you or him because what you say about him is some might say none too complimentary but perhaps we could go to page 20 in the B/C/S, top of the page, and page 13 in the English. And at the top of the page, we see that Mr. McCloskey says, "Oh, no, we are still learning, so we appreciate what you do. Okay. Where did Gvero fit in the command? What was his job as assistant commander for morale, legal and religious affairs? In fact I take it the 65th did not have a morale, legal and religious affairs person." And you say, "Yes, there was. I forgot about it. Assistant commander for that job was Major Milivoje Jankovic, assistant for morale, religious and legal." And just stopping there for a moment, what you say is right, presumably, Major Jankovic was the assistant commander for morale in your brigade or regiment, perhaps I should say?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. He was assistant for moral guidance, religious and legal affairs within the regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you say "In that group of the command of the regiment -- I'm so sorry, I simply forgot," because you'd forgotten about it earlier on in the interview; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the beginning of the interview, when Mr. McCloskey asked me about the regiment and how he was -- how it was organised, I simply omitted the assistant for moral guidance, religious and legal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And then Mr. McCloskey says, "It's all right. It's good to remember, because otherwise, you get stuck with Gvero." And you say, "just one question, if you don't mind," and Mr. McCloskey says, "Please." And you say, "No, I did not understand. I forgot the question that you've asked. I simply forgot it. Then we moved into this. So what was question before," and Mr. McCloskey repeats the question, "What was your understanding of what Gvero's duties and job was in the Main Staff? And I'm talking really what really -- what did he really do?" And could the B/C/S be scrolled down, please? And your answer is as follows: "Milan Gvero was director of the military high school that I went to in the fourth year of studies. As many people, I mean in their lives, they have nice, good opinion about their teachers and professors, and to be honest, most honestly, that kind of job, both in the JNA and in the VRS, I respected the least, me personally. To be honest, I don't really know what in practice they were doing except for some preparation for legal advice, some." And to stop there, why did you say you had the least respect for that type of job? As I say, I know this may be a little embarrassing, but be frank with the Chamber, if you would.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not anything disrespectful, but the closest way to describe it would be some animosity towards that type of work. I simply did not like that type of work. I don't know for what reason, whether I was traumatised for some reason from the period -- from the previous period of time. But I simply didn't like that type of work in the army. It had nothing to do with Mr. Gvero. I said that he was the principal of the school when I went to that school. I defended my graduation thesis before him. So I had a lot of respect towards him as a teacher, professor, and also as a senior officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page in the B/C/S, because the interview continues, and Mr. McCloskey deals with the matter from another angle and he asks you, "Well, he was the propaganda officer, wasn't he? The combat veterans may not like combat, I mean propaganda, but it's an important part of all military." And you say, "Yes. I understand. Not only that, I didn't respect them but I literally hated their part of job. My job, as a commander, everybody knows and they can see it. What propaganda? He was defeated. Gvero was defeated at the beginning of the war by someone who was not doing this kind of job ever." Expand on that, please, General.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When speaking of propaganda, what I was referring there was the fact that the assistant commander for moral guidance, religious and legal affairs, had no funds available to him to carry out any propaganda activities. One knows very well how effective propaganda is carried out, in order to achieve its aim. You have to have powerful media on your side. Not just at a local level. And he didn't have that type of media available to him, even in his own country. So what Republika Srpska did have was not available to Mr. Gvero. The state leadership did not put it at his disposal. That's what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And if we could scroll down, please, Mr. McCloskey goes on and says, "So what did -- what kind of propaganda did Gvero do?" And you say, "I really don't know. Logically, he was supposed to be doing some kind of information, informing their own troop, own forces, to have certain protocol duties of the army. If there was some big parades or celebrations, but there were not that many during the war." And in fact then the tape comes to an end and I can save everyone the bother of looking on, because at that point Mr. McCloskey moves on to a different topic. The answers that you gave at that time were presumably your true opinion of General Gvero; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And in the shortish period of time since that interview and today's date, has your opinion changed at all?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said previously, I'm not in the military service any longer, but when it comes to these specific questions, my position remains the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, sorry, I hate to interrupt you like this, Mr. Josse. Probably due to the line of questions adopted or followed by Mr. McCloskey, I think that the witness was at the time of his interview presented with two different stages in General Gvero's career. I want first to get this clear from the witness. The first question that he was asked and which he answered related to the function or the role that General Gvero filled at some point in time as director of the military high school. Am I correct in stating that when you said that you looked down on that role, you were specifically referring to the role or the function of the principal of the military high school and nothing else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour. In the period from 1977 to 1978. That's the period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So your opinion then, and now, would still be that there isn't much to say in favour of this role of director of the military high school, in your opinion? Just answer yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now you're putting me in an unpleasant situation. I didn't say anything bad about him as a person, Your Honours. As I have said previously, most of the people in the world harbour a positive opinion about their teachers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not referring to Mr. Gvero, your judgement of Mr. Gvero personally at the time. I'm referring only to your assessment of the role of the director of the military high school at the time. Your opinion was low, as regards that office, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we completely misunderstood each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you then make your position clear, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I mentioned the post held by General Gvero from that period of time. When I met him back in 1977, he was the director of the military secondary school. As I've told you earlier, at that time, I had no contact with Mr. Gvero except that I defended my graduation thesis before him. I did not speak about the office of the principal or director of the secondary school. I was not referring to Mr. Pujic, who held the office prior to Mr. Gvero, nor to Mr. Gvero.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but in the interview, you said, "To be honest, most honestly, that kind of job, both in the JNA and in the VRS, I respected the least, me personally." This you said in the context of explaining that at the time General Gvero was director of the military high school. So what job did you respect the least? What were you referring to when you said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was referring to the job of General Gvero in his role as assistant commander for moral guidance, religious and legal affairs. I was referring to the substance of that work, not to Mr. Gvero personally, and that pertained to 1992, when he was appointed to that post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That explains it and I don't need to go into the second point because when he dealt with propaganda that was only one aspect of General Gvero's function. So I think I have got it clear from you now, and Mr. Josse can proceed. Thank you, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I'm going to attempt to clarify this and define it a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What was the problem, as you saw it, with the role of the assistant commander for morale in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, I'm not talking about any difficulties when it comes to the role of assistant. I'm just sharing with you my personal position with regard to the substance of that job. Do you understand what I'm saying? I'm talking about a job that involves moral guidance, religious affairs. This is something completely new, something that had not existed before in the army. I'm talking about the substance of that work that inspires animosity in me. I simply don't care much about that type of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Am I right, General, that you, as a fighting man, really viewed morale as being created and led by the commander of a regiment rather than a man sitting behind a desk at the Main Staff? Is that the essence of it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I repeat for the last time, I'm not seeking to embarrass anyone, least of all my client, but why was it that you felt that morale needed to be done in the regiment itself rather than at the Main Staff level?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid that we are talking at cross-purposes here. I'm saying that the issue of morale can be best resolved by a commander, by way of his personal example. You can't have somebody explaining the goals of the fighting, theoretically and nothing of that sort can replace the role of a commander who should be guiding his troops. Just-- just presenting theories of how things should be done does not substitute real work on combat morale. No theory can replace that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps we could have a look at a document, please, 6D129. This is a document that emanated from General Gvero in June of 1992, headed, "Prevention of reprisal and treatment of journalists and representatives of international organisations." And near the top of the page, we see it says, "Such actions are not and must not be characteristic of members of our army because they tarnish the reputation and moral image of the Serbian soldier. We cannot allow improper conduct towards reprisals against innocents and helpless people merely because they are not Serbs." Is that sentence, the last sentence that I just read out, reflective, in your opinion, of the views of General Gvero?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is reflective of that. That's how I perceive him, and I believe that as a result of this position of his, he had problems with the state leadership of Republika Srpska. He was proclaimed as nostalgic of the former Yugoslavia and I believe that he entered into a conflict at an ideological level with the state leadership and so on and so forth. He was perceived as the advocate of the fraternity and unity ideas that had disappeared at the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Put another way, he, as far as you could ascertain, was a proponent of brotherhood and unity, which had existed in the JNA prior to its dispansion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And how did you become aware of the problems with the state leadership of the Republika Srpska? What was your knowledge of the problems that General Gvero had with the leadership?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was even a TV programme, a special TV programme on Serbian radio-television, or I don't know what its name was. In that programme, members of the inner state leadership appeared in that special programme and openly spoke about the problem that General Gvero had, and they portrayed him as being guilty of many things. They said that his place was not in the army. They tried to have him removed. In any case, I learned on the media about these problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would just like my learned friend at least to put the question to the witness in a way that we can ascertain specifically what period of time we are talking about or specific dates. This particular question was not put in that manner and it's unclear as to when the witness learned about the information he's testified to, and so I would just like the record to be clarified in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's a fair point.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour, I have not problem with that at all, perfectly reasonable observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When did you become aware of the dispute between -- it's Dr. Karadzic, isn't it, and General Gvero?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this was sometime in 1994, but believe me, it's very difficult for me to specify the month. This escalated in that year and continued until the end of the war. I believe that General Gvero was actually once or even more than once removed from his position. You have to understand that in conditions of war, there was very little possibility for regular information programmes and information did not reach us on a regular basis. It was pretty much a haphazard thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When you talk of General Gvero being a proponent of brotherhood and unity, please define, particularly for those of us who are not from the former Yugoslavia, what that meant.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The idea of brotherhood and unity meant equality among the peoples of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you have any dealings with General Gvero in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that up to mid-1995, I was hospitalised and I really can't remember whether I saw him that year. I suppose that we might have but it was only towards the end of 1995. I really cannot remember at the moment, but I'm sure that up to the 27th of July 1995, when I was in the western front, I really can't remember when I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: From any dealings with him, anything you read about him or by him, did you have any reason to conclude that General Gvero had ceased to believe in brotherhood and unity in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really did not have any information to the contrary. He -- General Gvero was already of a certain age when it is very hard to change one's opinions. So I would dare say that in his case, it was also the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you for your time, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Mr. Sarapa?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Savcic, I'm Djordje Sarapa and I appear for General Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: I'm going to have only a few questions for you and I believe it will be very simple for you to answer them. You just told us that you on the 27th of July 1995, you went to Krajina, to be more specific, this is the area of Drvar where you went; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Could you please tell us whether, during the course of August and September 1995, met Vinko Pandurevic and his brigade in the area of Grahovo and Drvar?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but let me be clear on this. This was not the Zvornik Brigade we are talking about. This was the 3rd Drina Brigade composed of several units of the Drina Corps, and the commander of that brigade, which was a temporary unit, a task force, so to speak, so the commander of that unit was Vinko Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Could you please tell us briefly what the task of your unit was, the one that you were in command of? And also what was the task of this brigade under Pandurevic's command? And could you also tell us what kind of fighting were you involved there?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 3rd Drina Brigade headed by Mr. Pandurevic arrived in the area at the beginning of August. They arrived in the Drvar sector, i.e. on the Drvar-Grahovo axis. Their task was to mount a defence on the line from the border of Republika Srpska Krajina on the right-hand side and mount Jadovnik on the left-hand side. The forces of the army of Republika Srpska that had manned those lines were broken up and the defence had to be stabilised. A manoeuvre detachment of that brigade, also known as wolves from the Drina, and my unit, carried out a reconnoitring activities and active combat activities in the direction of Grahovo. In front of us at that moment we had the Croatian army composed of the most elite units of the Croatian army that had previously taken Knin, i.e. the entire Republika Srpska Krajina. In other words, the fighting was against the Croatian army in the territory of the Republika Srpska, i.e. the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answers. I have no further questions for you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I -- yes, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask additional cross-examination of this witness just regarding the document shown to him during cross-examination of Borovcanin team. It is document P107. I have just few questions, not more than ten minutes perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Further cross-examination by Mr. Zivanovic:

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Savcic.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Yesterday you had an occasion to see Exhibit number P107, which is an order for active combat operations dated 2 July 1995. I believe you remember that document. We are talking about the operation Krivaja 95.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a different version of the same document but I believe that since we are talking about two versions of the same document, I believe that it would be best for you to look at both versions at the same time. That's why I would kindly ask the document to be provided to the witness on the ELMO. Could you please look at the version that you saw yesterday? It is on the screen, on the monitor, and if possible, at the same time, if you could show the other version that I've just provided? Is it technically feasible at all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Zivanovic, are you referring the witness or are you going to refer the witness to a particular part of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you indicate where is it, whether it's on the top, the middle or the bottom?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is page -- fifth page of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fifth, we are talking of --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Not this document but another one which I gave to Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But Madam Usher would need to know exactly which part from that page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is page 04303380.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which part of that page? Which paragraph, in other words?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is first paragraph, fourth line on this page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before that, sorry, can I see the ERN numbers of those two documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Of the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. It is fifth page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I just -- we will come to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: First page is -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why ERN number in e-court is different from both of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There is two version of the same document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What Judge Kwon is suggesting is that there isn't just two versions, that there is also another version. Which is the one on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, one at e-court and we asked to put it in e-court also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. What we are being told is the one on e-court supposedly is the one the witness was shown yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The ERN does not correspond.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, but it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that's why there are three versions --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- and not two.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Savcic, could you please look at line 4 of the document that is in front of you? Yesterday you had an occasion to read that document. But you saw the version in which this line was not crossed out.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're talking about the security organs of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Absolutely. I'm going to read it to you and you can just tell me whether I have read it out correctly. This sentence reads, "The security organs and military police will determine the sectors where prisoners of war and war booty will be collected." Do you agree that this sentence has been crossed out in this version?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it seems that in this version it has been crossed out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Do you see that on the upper margin of this page, it was added in handwriting and from that handwritten text to the crossed-out text, there is an arrow leading from the one to the other?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: I'm going to read to you the handwritten text and you tell me whether I have read it out correctly: "The sector of where war prisoners will be collected is the sector of Pribicevac"?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says in Pribicevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Yes in Pribicevac?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what is written.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Can you scroll down a little, please? Can you scroll up, please? Above that, you can see that it is also had written and also war booty?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the sector where prisoners of war and war booty will be collected is the sector of Pribicevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now when you look at this page, you will please see another sentence that has been crossed out a little bit below, maybe two lines below. Again I'm going to read it out and then you tell me whether I have read this sentence out correctly: "The security organ shall define and convey to the subordinated commands the application of the level of security in the area of combat activities."

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Is it also true that on both sides of this crossed-out lines, words "no;" is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: That's all. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Is this a document that you obtained from the Prosecution, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is from EDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So I take it there is a re-examination, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There is, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, please. How long do you expect it to last?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think about a half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good evening to you, Mr. Savcic. You were asked some questions initially --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You were asked some questions about General Gvero being a proponent of brotherhood and unity. Did you ever have a personal conversation with General Gvero about those particular views?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never discussed those views, but I am aware of those views because I know the man. I've known him for a number of years.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could I please show you 2756 in e-court? Before I ask you to go through this document, let me just ask you: Are you aware of what General Mladic's views were with respect to brotherhood and unity?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that they were very similar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One question. Yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How does that arise? I appreciate I cross-examined on brotherhood and unity but the fact that I cross-examined on that doesn't mean to say my learned friend is entitled to ask the witness about Mladic's view about that particular concept, I would submit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Would you like to comment on that, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Actually, I wouldn't. I think the question has already been answered, and I have another document that I'm prepared to present to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I also notice Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President, but these are larger areas that is more my specialty than Mr. Vanderpuye's and I can provide a clear response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we need to stop, stop the discussion on this. Let me confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question has been answered already but even if it hadn't, we have decided that we would have allowed it because it would -- it tends to shed light on what exactly General Gvero's views in respect of brotherhood and unity consisted in. So I don't know if you want to pursue the matter or not. Perhaps you can move to your next line of questions. Although you're free to pursue it if you want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think I can move ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I was showing you, I believe it was 2756. You were asked some questions about the relationship between General Gvero and the Supreme Commander. Is this 2756 or 2757 in e-court? 2757. Could I have, please, 2756 in e-court? All right. I think this is the correct document and if I could just direct your attention to the second paragraph, if we could just go down the page so he can read it.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Second paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one sentence? Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, the second full paragraph. I guess it's the third paragraph on the page. This is a communication to General Gvero from Dr. Radovan Karadzic. It's dated 17th of July 1995.
