In particular, I've referred you to the second paragraph in which it's indicated in this letter to the general that he's sabotaged the order relating -- pertaining to the information ministry's exclusive task of information and among other things has made unauthorised contact with international organisations without the presence and permission of authorised state organs and it invites the general to respond with respect to this non-compliance. Could I just show the witness the second page of this document? It's the next page, please. Now, were you -- have you had a chance to look at this page, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm looking at it. I've read it actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Were you aware of the disagreement or the dissatisfaction that the president had with the general's performance with respect to the discharge of his duties?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was disagreement, that General Gvero was under some pressure. As for the causes of this disagreement, I've already shared my opinion with you. I don't know whether this was due to the quality of his work, to the way he discharged his duties. I really wouldn't like to go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could please show the witness 2757 in e-court? This is a document that is dated 18th July 1995, which is the response to the previous document, from General Gvero. Have you had a chance to see that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am reading it now. I've not seen it before. I also would like to say that I have not seen the previous document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In this document, there is an indication from General Gvero that he's complied with all of the orders and evidence of that can be seen from the successes of the VRS in Srebrenica, Zepa and on other fronts. Do you see that on the document?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could, I'd just like to refer you to part of your cross-examination testimony with respect to some questions that were put to you by my friend Mr. Meek. In particular, he asked you some questions about the presence of senior officers in Nova Kasaba on the 13th of July 1995. In your response you indicated that you were aware that General Mladic was there and that he was -- and that nobody else was mentioned to you. Do you recall that response?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall my response.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you recall what you specifically told Mr. McCloskey during your October 2005 interview concerning what Major Malinic told you concerning the senior officers present at Nova Kasaba on 13th July 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, before you answer that question, yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This objection will require the witness to either leave the courtroom or to take his ear phones off. I don't know whether he understands any English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have a suspicion that he does. I watched him yesterday. You don't understand English at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I speak Russian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's remove the -- or if you prefer him to be out of the courtroom, we'll escort him out of the courtroom. It's as you prefer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm happy for him to take his ear phones off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know where this line of re-examination is going and of course I know what this interview says and I'm going to tell you in a moment, and I appreciate that one cross examines at one's peril. And in the interview, the witness suggests - the extent to which he suggests is a matter of some dispute - that General Gvero was in Nova Kasaba on that day. Now, we have assumed that that has never been the Prosecution's case. If the Prosecution are now in any way suggesting that that is their case, that General Gvero was there, then first of all, why haven't they led that evidence and why haven't they conducted the case on that basis? If it's not their case, why does it matter at all that the witness said that Malinic said that Gvero was at Nova Kasaba on that day? Perhaps I missed the point and I jumped up prematurely but it's a matter of course of real sensitivity and real importance as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I apologise. I do not like doing this but since he's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not regular, too. I mean usually I would ask the Defence witness -- Defence counsel whether they have any objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't. In fact the reason I was rising before was to say that from my point of view, I don't mind who responds to the submissions that I make personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Then go ahead, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, when he directs it at the Prosecution's case, that's something that I'm uniquely qualified to respond to that. We are in the midst of a -- what is in a redirect examination, and this tactic that counsel has used to give away the answers and provide the answers to the trier of fact is interesting, but I don't see how the Prosecution's case has anything to do with what this person will answer. First of all it goes to credibility, because we saw that he responded on, I believe it was cross, when asked by Mr. Meek, that General Mladic was the only one that Malinic said was there, and we know that he told me Gvero was there too. So it comes in purely for that reason, and whether it's part of our case or not is really irrelevant. He wants me to get into a larger picture and blunt the -- blunt what's going on here. I have no problem doing that, and I believe that there is evidence that General Gvero was in Nova Kasaba because of what this witness told me in Banja Luka. To the degree that you will take that evidence of what he heard Malinic say about General Gvero being in Nova Kasaba, I'm a realist. I don't think that proves he was there beyond a reasonable doubt. I think that shows that there is evidence that he was there and I think if you put it with all the other evidence that comes in in the Prosecution's case and the Defence case, it's going to be something I would like you to consider, but I would like to be able to have a chance for it to come into evidence in an appropriate way, without the bell being rung like it was by counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My response is, with respect, this is no way to prosecute a case. He says either he adduces it to impugn the credibility of his own witness, something which in my submission he's not entitled to do because it's his own witness, or he says it may ultimately be the Prosecution case that Gvero was there. Now, Your Honour, to some extent it's a fundamental issue as to the nature of the system that this trial is being conducted under, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we are going to get into this, can the witness leave the room because we are ready to roll our sleeves up and exchange personal cracks but if the -- it's not appropriate to have this in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't want this to go -- to escalate beyond what is reasonable. And I think we are soon going to tell you where we are heading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry. I mean, I was cut off. All I want to emphasise - I think I've done this already - is, as you can imagine, this is a matter of real importance and I repeat, I appreciate that one cross examines at one's peril but it's not a trivial matter whether General Gvero was at Nova Kasaba on that day, and if it does need -- if I've made an error of judgement and the witness should have left the courtroom in the first place, then I certainly apologise to the Chamber and in that also to my learned friend. But I perhaps made my submissions and I don't need to repeat them further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But I do emphasise that it's not a trivial matter from our point of view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Meek, did you want to make a contribution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might, just one thing, I think Mr. McCloskey may be mischaracterising my cross-examination and the witness's answer to a certain extent because on page 48 starting at line 24 going to 49 at line 2, Mr. McCloskey is putting forward that when I asked that General Mladic was the only one that Malinic said was there, and frankly my question was, and again it's on line 54 yesterday, that when you say the commander, isn't it true that Malinic told you that General Mladic had been there and had spoken to the prisoners of war on the soccer pitch on the 13th? My question was never was -- did Malinic tell you that General Mladic was the only one there? So I believe Mr. McCloskey has misspoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Re-examination doesn't necessarily arise only from the question. It arises also from the answer. But one moment. I need to confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Our decision is as follows: As I said, re-examination does not relate only to a question put on cross-examination but also to any statement made by the witness in answering those -- that particular question, which may go beyond the question itself. As we see it, we think that the question is a perfectly legitimate one and we also concede that it may also have to do with credibility issues. However, we also wish to make it clear that once this chapter is being opened - and General Gvero was certainly not mentioned when the witness answered that question when being cross-examined by Mr. Meek - you will have an opportunity to put further questions to the witness should you feel like, Mr. Josse, after the redirect is finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I don't want to complicate matters still further, but if Mr. Vanderpuye is going to take the witness to the relevant part of his interview, there is, we think, a translation issue and what I would invite him to do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then I think at this point in time, if you're going into details, I prefer the witness not to be here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, all I was going to do, Your Honour - see if we can do it this way - is the answer, the relevant answer, at the bottom of page 36 in the English, could I ask Mr. Vanderpuye to ask the witness to read it out in the original B/C/S so that it could be retranslated? If that's what he is -- I don't want to -- if he was proposing to deal with it in a different way, then it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Are we ready to go?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Because as you've said, I've always got the right to do that myself in due course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I was not going to accede to my learned friend's request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well. But he is --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think he is correct, he can put it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He is still free to do it himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As we said, that's why we reserved his right to further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Perhaps I should repeat my question, since it's been a while since I asked it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I had asked you do you recall specifically what you told Mr. McCloskey during your October 2005 interview concerning what Major Malinic told you about the senior officers present at Nova Kasaba on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether the question was formulated as to what Major Malinic had told me or whether I was asked whether I knew which officers of the Main Staff were there. I know that I replied that I knew that General Mladic was there and then I said, "I don't know, I think but I don't know for certain that General Gvero was there too."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me read back to you your response. Perhaps this will help you --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's my point. I would invite him to let the witness read it back in B/C/S, please, and it can be retranslated.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm simply asking him whether what I read him will refresh his recollection. That's independent of whether it's accurate, whether it's been accurately transcribed, et cetera. It's a completely separate issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And deal with it later, Mr. Josse. You can confront the witness later. Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honour, and I know you're going to overrule me, but if you go back to Mr. Vanderpuye's question to this witness now at line 24, page 47, he says, by my friend Mr. Meek, in particular he asked you some questions about the presence of senior officers in Nova Kasaba on 13th of July. If you look at my question, I never asked him about senior officers plural. I asked him about one officer, that was General Mladic, and frankly, Your Honour, the Prosecution had -- this is his witness, it's a Prosecution witness. They can ask the questions they want to. What they are doing, Your Honour, and I don't appreciate it, is they are bringing witnesses in front of this Tribunal and then they are trying to discredit them and show that they're not credible, and if they bring witnesses, Your Honour, that they know are not going to tell the truth or not going to be honest with the Court, then they shouldn't call them. It's not ethical.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, my concern is this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- matter's been translated to the witness and I think this is a huge problem at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not a huge problem at all. As I explained before, the right to re-cross -- re-examine the witness arises also from the answer given by him and not from only or exclusively the question. You may have and actually you did put the question as you put it, Mr. Meek, but the witness's answer went beyond that. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye? You were about to read to the witness part of his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If we could be able, we are put in a position to follow at least, is it available only in B/C/S or is it also in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There is an English translation of the statement, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And presumably, you're going to read from it, no? I don't think you read B/C/S, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No. I'm going to read from it. I have a hard copy. I'm just checking to see if there's one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I saw you wondering whether there was an English translation of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In e-court is the wonder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. In e-court it wouldn't be, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's 1D196.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 1D196. And if you could --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. What I was going to read was on the English transcript, page 36.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It should be lines 25 through 31.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The way we are going to proceed is you're going to read it in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's going to be translated by the interpreters in the -- in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I repeat, we do not accept this translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. This is precisely where I was heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We would give you the opportunity of the witness not having the B/C/S text in front of him now, and you can confront him with that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The -- just as a matter of -- just to be accurate, it is a transcription as opposed to a translation. That is, somebody wrote down the words that were actually spoken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's not discuss that in front of the witness. Let's move. Could you please read what you have there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yeah, sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then put your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The question was put to you: "What, if anything, later on did Malinic tell you about Beara?" Your answer was: "As far as I can remember Beara was not mentioned. He only said that on the 13th, Mladic appeared at the soccer field, he addressed war prisoners and Gvero was also appearing somewhere with TV crews." Question: "Where was Gvero appearing?" Answer: "In Nova Kasaba, both Gvero and Mladic. That was the only location that I'm talking about." Does that refresh your recollection as to what it is you told specifically Mr. McCloskey in 2005, October?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said just now, I told you what I remember saying, namely that I said that I know for a fact that General Mladic was there and as for General Gvero, I said that he may have been or that it seems to me that he was there. Those were the two formulations that I used, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: My question really goes to whether or not Major Malinic told you that General Gvero was there, not what you know independently of Major Malinic.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Malinic knows for a fact only that General Mladic was there, and if he, if somebody who was present on the spot says that he doesn't remember whether somebody else was there, then I certainly cannot claim that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Savcic. A few questions were put to you by my learned friend Mr. Petrusic on cross-examination concerning the attack on the Srebrenica enclave. Now, you correct me if I'm wrong but it appeared from your testimony that you were suggesting that there was not an attack on the Srebrenica enclave before July the 2nd. Is that the substance of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is not a true objection. I just want to draw your attention to the fact that I did not put questions to the witness about the attack on the Srebrenica enclave, but I rather put to the witness a document that speaks of the attack on the Srebrenica enclave. That document is 838, paragraph 2. This is why I ask that the Prosecutor rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: My question is just to the witness as to what his testimony with respect to that attack or attacks was. His recollection of what his testimony was. That's the extent of the question. I haven't implied anything in it. I just want to know if it's accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As I understand, Mr. Petrusic -- what he wants you to rephrase the first part of your question where you premised that few questions were put to you by my learned friend Mr. Petrusic concerning the attack on Srebrenica enclave. He's telling you, "I never put any questions as such on the attack on the Srebrenica enclave." So you need to rephrase that you can say yesterday you were shown a document which inter alia dealt with the Srebrenica attack on the Srebrenica enclave S it your position that before, June, July the 2nd, there was no attack on the Srebrenica enclave. I mean I've rephrased it for you and I think hopefully I have simplified matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You absolutely have.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if you've understood the learned Judge's question could you please answer it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood the question, Your Honours. I answered Mr. Petrusic's question only in relation to the written documents, not in relation to specific combat activities in Srebrenica and around Srebrenica. I'm not familiar with that. I went to Srebrenica only once in my life and that was sometime in 2000. Therefore, I do not know whether there were any attacks before the 2nd of July. I don't know anything else. In Bratunac, sometime in 1992, we defended ourselves from the attack launched in Srebrenica. As for everything else, I was not a participant in any other events and what I said pertained to the document, not to the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that, Mr. Savcic. You were asked some questions concerning the weaponry that was held or used by the Muslim forces during the Zepa operation. Now, with respect to that weaponry, I think those questions were put to you by my learned friend Mr. Josse, and he'll correct me if I'm wrong. Now, what I'd like to know is what weaponry did you have at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered that question too when asked by somebody from Defence. What we used was infantry weapons, equipment for close anti-armour combat which are hand-held rocket launchers. I also had two firing groups of mortars, 120 millimetres, and two -- and also cannons B 176 millimetres. This is what we used. Rather this is what I used. I don't know whether other people used something else. I don't think they did. As I told you, this is a very inaccessible terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I do have a document I'd like to show the witness but I see that it's 5.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You still have another quarter of an hour. Our break is at quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Could I have 251 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Same observation that Mr. Vanderpuye made in relation to some of my questions, could we have a time frame in relation to that last question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Correct. He is going to show up a document in any case, I suppose, that it would be dated. Is that right, Mr. Vanderpuye, or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The document is dated.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: But before I show it to you, let me just ask you: Are you aware of whether or not chemical weapons were used or whether you had chemical weapons at your disposal to use? And this is in July of 1995, on or around the 21st.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have chemicals weapons except for a very limited amount of police gases, which were intended to be used against large number of people in the proper police circumstances, which are used in every country when dealing with crowds. Thus, except for these gases, typically used by police, I'm not aware of anything else that we had. These police gases were used by me twice, and both times against Serbian forces when we had to re-establish control.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Can I please show you 2517 in e-court, please? All right. Mr. Savcic, this is a document that's dated the 21st of July 1995. It is -- if we go to the bottom of it, I think we can see -- all right. We can see that it is issued by General Tolimir. I want to refer you, if I could, to paragraph numbered 4. In that paragraph states that "We believe we would be in a more advantageous position for direct negotiations after we inflict losses on enemy's military personnel. We request means for crushing enemy defence in the areas of Brezova Ravan and Purtici." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The translation is e-court is different to the one that was read out. "Manpower" is used rather than the word that my learned friend used. It's something that needs to be sorted out in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I appreciate that. I'll read it right out of e-court then. I think I have a slightly different version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, go ahead. Thank you, Mr. Josse and Mr. Vanderpuye. That's the word we have in front of us as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In any event, I would refer you to paragraph 5 where you can probably see it says, "The most convenient means for their destruction would be the usage of chemical weapons or aerosol grenades and bombs." Is this consistent with the chemical weapons that you've described that were available to you during that particular campaign?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, I didn't say that that was at our disposal during combat. In order to understand this better, these police poisonous gases for temporary disablement of enemy require that certain weapons exist in order for them to be used. One has to have a chemical rifle Shermalin [phoen] and it cannot be used in the open space at all. This is what I was referring to. These types of equipment. I have no knowledge of any other weapons or equipments. I did not use them myself because in the open space they are of no use.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could you just tell us first what is an aerosol grenade?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have it in the military police. We did not use it. And I'm not familiar with it. I don't know what this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And so when General Tolimir has made this apparent proposal to use chemical weapons, do you have any understanding of what it is he's talking about in this document?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly do not understand what he had in mind, what he proposed. What I know for certain is that in addition to the equipment that I mentioned several times already, I did not hear of others, nor did I know that they existed in the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, if you look at the last paragraph where it says, "We believe that we could force Muslims to surrender sooner if we would destroy groups of Muslims refugees fleeing from the direction of Stublic, Radava and Brloska Planina," does that give you an idea as to what this proposal is about?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These sectors mentioned here were quite far away from our forces. As far as I could see, the date, it was the 21st of July, correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct. And we could just maybe zoom out a little bit so we can all see it.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The positions that were held on the 21st of July, the positions of the army of Republika Srpska and the Zepa Brigade, were the same as those on the 15th of July in the afternoon. Only the line in the direction of Gusanica was moved. So physically we were unable to reach the civilians fleeing. Between that population and our forces there were the forces of the Zepa Brigade who were present there, just like in the beginning of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that, Mr. Savcic. I wanted to have P0005 in e-court, please. And I can refer you to page 15 on the B/C/S version and page 10 on the English version. All right. Maybe I can direct your attention to the paragraph on this page referring to the Drina Corps and I believe you were asked some questions about that on cross-examination. Are you familiar with this paragraph, Mr. Savcic? Correct me if I'm wrong, but from your testimony on cross-examination, it appeared that you suggested that the order that was issued on 2nd July 1995 changed the directive that was issued to the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because in the order on July the 2nd, it says that the task of the Drina Corps was to carry out, as soon as possible, complete physical separation of Srebrenica and Zepa and to narrow down, which is missing here, to narrow down the Srebrenica enclave to the urban area. And you can see that it's missing in the task given to the Drina Corps in the directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I see. So you would agree, then, that the objective of the operations that were directed -- that the Drina Corps engage in, which, as is written in this document, is to prevent communication between individuals in the two enclaves by a planned, well-thought-out combat operation and create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa, you would agree that that objective is in fact in the order that was issued on July the 2nd, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the task given to the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The objective in the July 2nd order that you looked at was to reduce those enclaves to their urban areas; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To separate and to reduce. That was the task, the task that was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the objective of that task was to create conditions for the elimination of the enclaves, right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This is a cross-examination, in our submission, this series of questions indicate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the -- yes, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'll just put the other document up. Maybe he can read that. I think it would probably be more efficient for me to read it than to put it on the ELMO and -- or in e-court and have the witness read the document and ask him what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the gist of the line of questions is to find out whether, indeed, they were different or not, but I'll need to consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We think that insofar as Mr. Josse's objection indicates that you are using a leading question, then he is perfectly correct. So that -- the way you choose to do it is your problem. We are not going to tell you how to do it. But I think you need to rephrase your question in the first place. And it's time, anyway --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- for the break. So we will have a 25-minute break starting from now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. After reviewing the record and conversing with my colleagues, I'm going to move to a different area, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked several questions about the movement of the population in and around Zepa in mid-July. I want to put to you a few questions concerning that. I have a document here, it's an UNPROFOR document, it's dated July 15th, there is no translation for it but let me put to you this. Throughout the week, meaning the week preceding the 15th of July -- the 65 ter number is 2875. "Throughout the week," meaning the week preceding the 15th of July, "there had been sporadic artillery, mortar and heavy machine-gun fire directed at the safe areas' population centres, particularly Zepa town and the villages of Riovici [phoen] and Perpecki [phoen]. Last Saturday, 8th July, the Bosnians asked UNPROFOR to return the 127 weapons that had been handed over to UNPROFOR following the demilitarisation agreement of 8th May 1993. The weapons were released but were not assessed to be of any significant military value." Were you aware of that particular situation as I've just read it to you?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the sporadic activities, I told you that I arrived on the 14th of July. I told you what I did and I also I told you what I did between the 15th and the 24th and 25th. I elaborated on that. I told you what equipment and weaponry I used. Anything beyond that I really wouldn't be able to tell you anything about because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Is it your testimony that you were completely unaware of the situation that existed at the time that you arrived in the area of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a general idea of the situation. I arrived after the attack that ensued, not in the territory of Zepa but on the separation line between the warring parties. The village of Zepa is somewhat further away from that very line.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me ask you -- I'm going to read to you some other facts as are indicated in this document. "UNPROFOR's position in the pocket has also been difficult. The 79 Ukrainians in the pocket have been under Serb bombardment since the 27 June with the tempo increasing this week. Earlier in the week the Serbs tried to force the Ukrainians out of OP 9 at the southern end of the pocket. Later in the week OPs 1, 2 and 3 at the south-western end of the pocket were also attacked." Do you have any knowledge of those circumstances and did you have that knowledge at the time that you arrived?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any knowledge about this. On 27th of July [as interpreted], I was still at the command post in Crna Rijeka and I really didn't know what was going on on the confrontation line. I know that my forces did not have any support, they did not have any artillery support, that is, that would enable them to shell any areas at any considerable distance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm told the witness said June, as would make more sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. You did say 27th of June and not 27th of July, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that it says here, in line - how do you do that - 66, 2, that I said 27th of July. Maybe I misunderstood Mr. Prosecutor's question. The shelling that is mentioned here when the 79 Ukrainians were exposed to the Serb shelling, something that happened on the 27th of June? Is that what you were asking me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct. What I wanted to know is if you had knowledge of that or came into knowledge of that in and around the time that you were in the Zepa area.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer was clear. On the 27th of June, I was still at the command post in Crna Rijeka. I remember that on the 26th was the day when there was this attack on the command post of the Main Staff and I really didn't know what was going on somewhere else, away from the position where I was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you know on the 15th of July that the 79 Ukrainians that are referred to in this document had been under bombardment since 27th of June?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not exposed to bombardment. Our officers, General Mladic and General Tolimir were in direct contact with Lieutenant-Colonel Dunik, the commander of the UNPROFOR. They were in daily contact and I don't remember him complaining of any incorrect doings on our part, especially not of any bombardment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you know, in July, around July 15th, did you know that these attacks on the OPs, OP 9, OP 1, OP 2 and OP 3, came after the delivery of an ultimatum on the 30th of June?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of the position of these features that you're referring to and I really don't know who was it who gave any ultimatum, so I can't tell you anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. If I'll just refer you to another -- another area for a moment. You were asked some questions about whether or not specifically check-point number 2 in Boksanica was under the control of the VRS or under UNPROFOR's control and I want to put this to you. It's 2671. It's 2671 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Having had a moment to think about it, it may be semantics and if it is, I apologise, but is my learned friend allowed to say, "I want to put this to you? Isn't he allowed to show the witness a document and invite the witness to comment upon it? Because the questions that have preceded that, he's asserted facts. The witness, for the most part, hasn't even accepted those facts or had no knowledge of them. He needs to be a bit careful bearing in mind this is a re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I appreciate my learned friend's comments. I don't subscribe to them, however. I think I've put the facts to the witness in a fair way for the witness to pass on. I haven't led the witness. I haven't invited a particular response or an answer. I've simply asked him to comment on it as it has arisen directly out of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know if this is a case of two great countries divided by the same language. So I'm not sure whether it's semantics as well, Mr. Josse. I haven't got it clear in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm not asking for a ruling, Your Honour. It was an observation and I will continue to observe the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for your eagle eyes, Mr. Josse. Let's proceed. I think we got the message as to what you wanted to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's proceed, but thank you, Mr. Josse, for the observation .

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I wanted to do is refer the witness if I could to the paragraph if we could just page down a little bit, okay, to the paragraph following UNPROFOR which you can hopefully see on your screen. That paragraph reads, "Check-point number 2 Boksanica where UNPROFOR commander or the UNPROFOR commander is located has been put under the control of our forces. An agreement was reached with him not to attack with the condition that they should not open fire on our battle formation B/B, which he accepted with a request to leave his positions where they are and he would in return provide information on enemy activity and would not call in NATO air force."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you aware of those circumstances on or around the 15th of July when you were in the area of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of the presence of the NATO air force, a comical situation arose as a result of combat inexperience. The aircraft at first flew at the speed, sonic speed. We sought shelter, but later on, we realised that they were not going to engage. This is not my document. I told you a while ago what the position was at this UNPROFOR check-point in Boksanica. Lieutenant-Colonel Dunik was there all the time. He maintained contact with his forces in Zepa, he would go to Zepa, he would go back to the check-point and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Could we just page up for a moment? All the way up to the top, please. Thank you very much. Are you able to determine, are you able to read to whom this communication is addressed?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, I don't know what this GSSRS stand for. It was sent to the forward command post of the Drina Corps and the command of the 65th Motorised Regiment and this is a combat report which was apparently sent to me by the brigade which is quite odd.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Just bear with me for one moment, Mr. Savcic. Just bear with me for one moment, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, and thank you, Mr. Savcic. I have no further redirect examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Josse, would you like to put any further questions to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Further cross-examination by Mr. Josse:

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could we have 1D196 back in e-court? And it's page 56 in the B/C/S and 36 in the English. I want you, General, to cast your mind back to this interview. And I want to go through in some detail with you the procedure that was adopted in that interview. Mr. McCloskey speaks English, you speak Serbian, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, save for some Russian, I don't speak any other foreign languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There was one interpreter present; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So that we all understand, that interpreter was not interpreting simultaneously. In other words, Mr. McCloskey would ask his question, that would be translated into Serbian, you would then give an answer in Serbian and that would be translated back into English?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the procedure, precisely so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And a tape was running of everything that all the participants to the interview said at all material times?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, we can see that Mr. McCloskey asks a question four lines down on the page that we have in front of us. This question therefore was asked in English and what we see here, tell me if you're able to agree with this, is what was translated to you by the interpreter at the time. In other words, it's not what Mr. McCloskey said but it's what the interpreter interpreted Mr. McCloskey as having said, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. Otherwise, we would not have been able to communicate.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we do not have a language in common, do we?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Indeed. Could you read out Mr. McCloskey's question as translated to you, slowly, please?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this the question starting with "later"? "Later in the conversation with Malinic, did he tell you anything? Did he tell you anything in relation to Beara?" Is this what you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That was what I had in mind. And I'm now going to ask you to read out your reply, but please do this extremely slowly because it's a translation of this answer that General Gvero's Defence is particularly concerned about. So very slowly, please. I would do it for you but I have the same disadvantage as Mr. McCloskey. I'm afraid I don't speak or read your language.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer reads, "To Beara, to be honest, I don't remember because on that day, the 13th of July, only General Mladic arrived there. He addressed this -- these prisoners of war, and as far as I know, and it seems to me that somewhere there, General Gvero might have appeared with some TV crews."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So in your answer, you used the words "as far as I know"?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And "it seems to me that somewhere there, General Gvero might have appeared."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, it's right, isn't it, that that information that you relayed in that answer came from a conversation that you had had with Major Malinic?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But kindly bear in mind that this took place in 2005, which means ten years after the events, and to be honest with you, I really can't remember save for the conversation on the 27th of July, and when I stayed there for some half an hour, we talked about that, but this was not something that came up very often in our conversations, and in any case, we did not see each other that often to be able to discuss things at any length.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In your examination-in-chief, you told the Trial Chamber when being questioned by Mr. Vanderpuye that you had had a conversation more recently with Major Malinic about the subject matter of your testimony. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I didn't say recently.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When was that conversation, please?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. Maybe a few months after my interview in Banja Luka with Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And at that time, or during that conversation, did you discuss General Gvero at all?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Believe me, I was only interested in whether Malinic remembered whether he had received that telegram that is in dispute that we have discussed here, whether he remembered that, and then he confirmed to me that he was sure that he had not received that telegram. As for any other details, believe me, we absolutely didn't discuss any.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: At that time, when you had that conversation with Malinic, were you under the impression that Malinic was going to be a Prosecution witness in this case?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know -- actually I don't know whether he had already received the summons, whether he had already been interviewed. I was not aware that he might appear as a witness in these proceedings, but it would have been only more logical for somebody who was a participant in the events to provide some answers rather than somebody who knew of the events from second or third hand as a hearsay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And as you sit here today and give your evidence, are you aware that the Prosecution have made a conscious decision not to call Major Malinic in this case and have dropped him from their witness list?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, before you answer the question, please, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I object to the question. It has no basis or relation to the redirect examination that was conducted or relevancy to this witness's testimony in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It goes to his state of mind, in our submission, in relation to the various answers he's given as to General Gvero's alleged presence at Nova Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The statement that is at issue was made in 2005 and so unless my learned friend wants to establish what the witness's state of mind was in relation to the specific time that the statement was made, it is irrelevant to these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop, stop, because we have the witness here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are unanimous here. We don't see the relevance here so we suggest you move to your next question, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There are no further questions, although I will have some submissions about the matter which can be dealt with when we deal with exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Josse. General, we've come to the end of your testimony. We have no further questions for you, which means that you are free to go. Our staff will assist you. Before you leave the courtroom, however, on behalf of the Trial Chamber and the Tribunal, I wish to thank you for having come over and also I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Documents. Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. For the direct examination, we have no documents. They have all been already admitted or marked for identification. As to the redirect examination, I have P02756, P02757, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. One is the Karadzic and the other one is the Mladic -- no. Gvero -- Karadzic to Gvero, Gvero to Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections? Mr. Josse, you still have some energy left.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I'm in a position now to deal with Colonel Trkulja's exhibits. So far as these are concerned, again, I would appreciate a little time to think about them. Your Honour, they were used in re-examination and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The first one was used in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The first one was used --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have -- sorry to butt in like this but I haven't 2756 and 2757.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it was used in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Haven't 2756 and 2757 been already tendered?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think one of them, I think one of them should -- there is an attempt to have it tendered through the last witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So in fact sorry, Your Honour, I'm literally thinking aloud. The submissions I'm going to make about Trkulja will cover Malinic as well, so I'm actually happy to submit in relation to both of them if the Court is ready for that. It will take me a few moments' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it's okay, Mr. Josse. In the meantime can we dispose of the documents that two of the Defence teams wish to tender with this document -- with this witness? One is from the Popovic Defence team and it's document ID382.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, 1D382.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 1D, sorry, 1D382. Any objection? This is order for active combat activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There is no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. No objection from the other Defence teams so it's admitted. Then there is the Borovcanin Defence team who wishes to tender three documents, namely 4D120, 4D8, 4DP8 and 4D1D197. The details of these documents have been circulated. Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There is no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic? Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a sentence, Your Honours. 4D120 is still awaiting translation and we were told it would be ready on Monday and it would be in the system on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. No objection, so these are all admitted and obviously in relation to 4D120, it will be marked for identification to be upgraded to full admittance once the translation has been filed or made available. Okay. Mr. Josse, to make it clear, we are now moving -- yes, Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, since we are dealing with the tendering of documents through Witness Savcic, the Defence of General Miletic tenders into evidence P35 -- which is already in the system under P1033, which is the order dated the 13th of July 1995. The Defence used it during cross-examination of this witness. In addition to this, I wish to draw attention of the Chamber to the fact that P838, which the Defence also used in cross-examination, is already in the system under number P107. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrusic. Perhaps we could verify-- P1033 hasn't been admitted already? Or -- please two documents, P35, which is also P1033, any objection? I don't know if it has been tendered already. This is what I asked. Sometimes it's in the system without having been tendered. Having a 65 ter number. It hasn't been tendered, you see, no, it hasn't. So any objection, Mr. Vanderpuye? To either of tease two documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We are having some trouble identifying which document it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It has two numbers. Madam Fauveau, I'm sure, will help us. I saw her --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It might -- if she had actually a copy I could just look at it briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the document which was on the Prosecution list. This is document typed up by General Mladic and we do not oppose to showing a copy to my learned friend should he wish to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you have simplified it sufficiently well to avoid having --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There is no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. No objection to that. And the other one was 838? Can you repeat the number, please, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second one is P838, which is identical to P107, which has already been admitted and this is the order of General Zivanovic dated the 2nd of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we need it tendered again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No objection to that either. It's fine as it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Any other Defence team wishes to tender any other document with this witness, Savcic? None? All right. Do you think you can finish your submissions in ten minutes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. I think I can, Your Honour, save one thing which I'll come to at the end. Could I begin by making it clear that I am slightly loathe to make submissions on points of principle when I'm about to concede that take the two examples the two documents in relation to the last witness Savcic that the Prosecution wished to introduce, they are clearly important documents in the case of General Gvero, and they are clearly going to be admitted into evidence at some point in time. And as I've already said, one of those appears on the Trkulja list as well. So far as they are concerned, and the Trkulja documents are concerned, the witnesses in question had no knowledge of any of those documents and really it's up to the Trial Chamber, as to the extent to which they want to keep a tight rein on the exhibits introduced into this case. Hitherto, tight control has been placed on the parties introducing documents, particularly where disagreement occurs. Where a witness says that he knows nothing about a document, in reality, we submit, it's exactly the same as if that document was being tendered from the bar table rather than through the witness. That is particularly true when the party calling the witness is doing that. It's rather different if the opposing party does it to impugn the credibility of the witness. Now, the issue as to whether the Prosecution are entitled to impugn the credibility of their own witnesses is a very big issue and not one that I'm going to address now. It's alluded to in the motion filed yesterday jointly by the Defence teams in relation to 65 ter documents used in re-examination. It's paragraphs, I think -- excuse me, I don't have a note of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. And the Trial Chamber, in our submission, really need to decide whether the Prosecution are entitled to do what they are purporting to do. So far as the list in front of me is concerned, we would invite those three documents put to Trkulja, which were not on the 65 ter list, to be marked for identification pending the resolution of the motion filed yesterday. So far as the other three documents are concerned, my submission yet again is more by way of an observation. It is up to the Trial Chamber. But in reality this way of going about things is no more than the parties simply saying, "Here is a document, we wish it to be admitted into evidence." But, Your Honour, I do concede that all of these documents, subject to authenticity, which isn't the issue here, are documents which are contemporaneous and prima facie relevant and admissible in this case. To say otherwise would be absurd. And could I contrast that, and this is where I said I may need more than ten minutes, you might recall that on the 27th of August, it was a Monday, Mr. Thayer said that he had reached an agreement with the Defence, primarily with me, frankly, in relation to various Zepa documents and he, and I make no criticism of him in this regard, is no doubt still in the process of preparing those. He then asked the Trial Chamber to consider admitting P528, which is the 107-page United Nations report on the events in Srebrenica. That having now considered the matter, I do oppose strenuously and will need a bit more time to develop. But the reason I'm mentioning it now is it really fits into the submission that I'm just making because I do have to concede that that document, which is a report of events prepared years after the events, is in stark contrast to these particular documents. But it's more a question of how the Trial Chamber is content with contemporaneous documents being introduced into evidence, and we submit that if a witness is shown a document, particularly by the party who calls that witness, and the witness says, "I know nothing about it," that's an improper way for a document to be so admitted into evidence. Perhaps the Trial Chamber will schedule a short period of time in due course for us to argue 528. I would invite the Prosecution to go first in relation to that when it is scheduled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour's microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just clarify this. Which are the three documents that you wish or ask to be marked for identification only for the time being pending the resolution of the joint urgent motion filed yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The three that Ms. Stewart very helpfully marked with a double asterisk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, can I ask you a question? I'm attracted by the words you used near the end here, "particularly by the party who called the witness." Are you drawing a distinction between documents put to a witness in cross-examination, for example, where the witness's response is "I've never seen the document before, and I don't know anything about it," because I have a strong recollection of several documents of that nature going in through the cross-examination with those kinds of responses. Are you saying there is a distinction, whether it's the party calling the witness or the party cross-examining the witness as to the admissibility of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, I am. I have to do that partly for the reason that Your Honour has just indicated but I also do it because we maintain that the party calling a witness is not entitled to impugn the credibility of their own witness. We have seen a great deal of that over the last few days. And whether these exhibits is the way to grapple with frankly that difficult evidential issue, I don't know. Probably not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: I'm just trying to ascertain if the essence of your argument is that the document can't go in if the witness is not familiar with it when the witness's credibility is being impugned or if you're saying it's a more general principle, that the party calling the witness can't introduce a document through that witness if the witness says he doesn't know anything about it as distinct from a party cross-examining.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Only when the party calling the witness is impugning the credibility of their own witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: So that limited category, not when they use it for some other purpose, perhaps just to expand on an area of cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey, you've got two minutes. If you prefer to speak tomorrow we will adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can take the two minutes. I think the issue of the UN report, Mr. Thayer will be prepared to argue with Mr. Josse tomorrow. I would just like to give our view point on this idea of impugning the credibility so you see where both sides are coming from and perhaps if need be we with argue further on it, but it's the Prosecution's view point that a party can always impugn his own witness now. This idea or this concept that one cannot impugn its own witness is an ancient concept that goes back to the roots of the adversarial system that in most jurisdictions that I'm aware has been set aside. The term "hostile witness" has now been rejected. It's been replaced by "an adverse witness." So I think we are a bit old fashioned on the other side here and as I said in my opening statement, as we said in our trial brief, many of our witnesses were directly involved in the events and they will be not being completely credible with Your Honours, and that I think we should all face the reality that what is going on here, especially when we see -- when a witness -- when we -- when a witness is taken by the Defence in an area completely outside of the direct, which we understand and we generally don't object to, and is led, that this is fundamentally the Defence calling the witness and we would rather have it be done now frankly than later. And so when we are questioning Mr. Savcic, for example on the areas it's fundamentally cross-examination and it's not more than -- it is cross-examination. We've chosen not to take the leading question route in most cases because of the President's preference, and the fact that I think leading questions sometimes aren't the most reliable questions in the world. We get -- sometimes we get more reliable answers from non-leading questions, so we have chosen not to take that but I think we need -- the reality is this is cross-examination. So that's our view point on it. If you want to hear us any further on it I'm sure we can talk for a long time but as for the documents, tomorrow is another day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Tomorrow I take it we'll discuss this. We'll discuss also the UN report, 528.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Will you have the next witness available tomorrow, Blazkic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He is available. He is our witness that we have been saving for when we need him. So we can bring him on tomorrow if you'd like or we can just argue tomorrow. However you -- we are ready to go or he could go Tuesday. I might get a break on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see there is anxiety on the faces of some of the Defence teams. You wish to have the witness come first and then we discuss the rest later, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: All I can say is I like an argument, but I don't think I can keep the argument going all of tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
